title: Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) Procedures for the Management of the Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry
summary: Defines the procedures IANA uses when handling requests to the Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number registry, and explains the rationale behind them. It updates IANA's procedures and replaces earlier UDP and TCP port assignment procedures. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: Port numbers are like apartment numbers for programs. This is the rulebook IANA follows when someone asks for a number or name, written so the limited supply lasts a long time.

subtitle: The rulebook IANA follows when handing out service names and port numbers for TCP, UDP, SCTP and DCCP.

tldr.problem: Rules for assigning service names and port numbers were scattered across web forms, registry headers and an old guidelines RFC, with no procedure for returning, reusing or revoking assignments.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6335 defines one process for all transport protocols: a strict service name syntax, three port ranges, assignment only for the transports requested, and procedures for de-assignment, reuse, revocation and a ban on transfers.
tldr.outcome: It makes the registry the single authority for service names and ports, aimed at conserving the finite port space. It obsoletes Sections 8 and 9.1 of RFC 2780 and is a Best Current Practice.

today: RFC 6335 is a Best Current Practice and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It updates RFC 2780, RFC 2782, RFC 3828, RFC 4340, RFC 4960 and RFC 5595.

sections.title: Why the Procedures Were Rewritten
sections.content:
Assigning service names and port numbers for TCP and UDP had long had unclear guidelines. Newer transports, the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) and the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP), and mechanisms such as DNS SRV records each had separate registries and rules. There were also no documented procedures for modification, revocation or release.

RFC 6335 establishes identical assignment procedures for all IETF transport protocols, including future ones. It obsoletes Sections 8 and 9.1 of RFC 2780 and updates the procedures for DCCP and SCTP. UDP-Lite shares the UDP port space, so it is updated too.

It also merges two older name lists, an informal one of roughly 500 service names kept outside IANA and the IANA Protocol and Service Names registry, into the IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number registry, which becomes the single authoritative registry. The internal procedures of the Expert Review team are not documented in any RFC, and this document does not change that.
sections.eli5: The lists of who owns which number were kept in several places and nobody knew how to give a number back. This document puts all the rules in one place.

sections.title: How Ports and Service Names Are Used
sections.content:
Ports serve two purposes: they differentiate transport sessions between the same pair of endpoints, and they may identify the application protocol or service. Ports are 16-bit numbers, and the source and destination ports together with the IP addresses identify a session. Port 23 is known as telnet, and port 80 as http.

A port number implying a service is ultimately a local decision. Several instances of a service cannot generally listen on one port, and hosts behind one NAT gateway cannot all map the same external port. Applications may use port numbers directly, look them up by name, query DNS SRV records, or use other methods.

Because the port space is finite, applying for only a service name without a fixed port is RECOMMENDED whenever possible. This suits applications that find ports at run time through SRV records.
sections.eli5: A port is like an apartment number: the building address gets you to the computer and the number gets you to the right program. If you can ask for the number when you arrive, you do not need to reserve one.

sections.title: Service Names
sections.content:
The service name is the unique key in the registry and can also be used in DNS SRV records. Where an SRV record needs a service label, it MUST be a service name with an underscore prepended, and the name SHOULD be registered with IANA.

A valid service name:

  • MUST be 1 to 15 characters long;
  • MUST contain only US-ASCII letters, digits and hyphens;
  • MUST contain at least one letter, so it cannot be confused with a port or a port range;
  • MUST NOT begin or end with a hyphen, and hyphens MUST NOT be adjacent.

Case is ignored, so http and HTTP are the same. Names are opaque identifiers, so owning Example-Foo gives no claim to other names starting with Example-. Names should be brief and avoid redundant words such as "port" or "service".

Several names can share a port, called overloading. The RFC's example is port 3478 with the names stun and turn. The name http also has the synonyms www and www-http, but only http should be used in SRV records.
sections.eli5: A service name is a short nickname for a program, using letters, numbers and dashes, never longer than 15 characters. Capital letters do not matter.

sections.title: Port Number Ranges
sections.content:
The 16-bit port space for TCP, UDP, UDP-Lite, SCTP and DCCP has three ranges:

  • System Ports (Well Known): 0-1023, assigned by IANA.
  • User Ports (Registered): 1024-49151, assigned by IANA.
  • Dynamic Ports (Private or Ephemeral): 49152-65535, never assigned.

In the assignable ranges (0-49151) each number is Assigned, Unassigned or Reserved. Reserved numbers are not available for regular assignment, and include values at the edges of each range such as 0, 1023 and 1024. IANA typically lists only Assigned and Reserved entries.

Ports 1021 and 1022, with service names exp1 and exp2, are for experimentation. They are hard to restrict, so users SHOULD take measures to confirm they are talking to the intended process, for example by including a 64-bit nonce.
sections.eli5: The numbers are split into three neighborhoods: a small one for famous programs, a big one you can apply to live in, and one anyone can borrow for a moment but nobody owns.

sections.title: Principles for Managing the Registry
sections.content:
The core principle is to conserve the port space. At the time of writing about 9% of the User Port space was assigned, at roughly 400 ports per year, which the RFC says could sustain another 85 years of assignment if conservation continues.

IANA strives to assign one port per service, one for all variants of a service, one for all device types in the same service, and to encourage secure protocols. Services are expected to demultiplex internally, for instance by carrying version information in-band.

The biggest change: IANA now assigns a port only for the transport protocols named in the request. The same number is marked Reserved for the others, and the Assignee must ask IANA to convert it before using another transport. This ends the old practice of assigning both TCP and UDP automatically. Applications SHOULD request only the transports they use. The RFC notes that IANA is not strictly bound by these principles.
sections.eli5: Because there are not endless numbers, you only get a number for the way you actually travel. A number for the bus is not automatically yours for the train.

sections.title: Assignment and Lifecycle Procedures
sections.content:
A request supplies a Service Name, Transport Protocol(s), Assignee, Contact, Description and Reference (all REQUIRED), plus optionally a Port Number, a DCCP Service Code (required for DCCP only), Known Unauthorized Uses and Assignment Notes. The requester MUST NOT deploy a requested port on the public Internet before assignment is complete.

Requests that ask for a port number go to Expert Review. Requests for a service name only are assigned on a First Come First Served basis. A User Port request MUST explain why a Dynamic Port is unsuitable. A System Port request MUST explain why both Dynamic and User Ports are unsuitable, and is granted only under IETF Review or IESG Approval.

  • De-assignment: the Assignee can return a port at any time and it becomes Reserved. Service names are RECOMMENDED to stay assigned.
  • Reuse: treated as de-assignment followed by new assignment, with a new service name. Reusing a service name is NOT RECOMMENDED.
  • Revocation: IANA-initiated, only for overwhelming need, after a four-week community call. Revoking service names is NOT RECOMMENDED.
  • Transfer: not permitted, even between consenting parties; use a coordinated release and new assignment.

Disagreements follow the appeals process in RFC 5226.
sections.eli5: To get a number you fill in a form and explain why you need it. You can give it back, but you cannot sell it to a friend; your friend has to apply on their own.

sections.title: Security and IANA Actions
sections.content:
The procedures do not change the security properties of UDP, TCP, SCTP or DCCP. An assigned port does not endorse an application, and traffic on an assigned port is not necessarily "good" traffic or even the assigned service. Firewall and system administrators should configure systems from their knowledge of the traffic, not from whether a name or number is assigned. Separate assignments for secure and insecure variants of the same service are to be avoided.

For IANA, the document merges the independent service name registry into the official one, creates service names for Protocol and Service Names entries that lacked one, and marks www and www-http as duplicates of http. Existing short names with illegal characters, about 2% and 96 names in all, got new well-formed names with illegal characters replaced by hyphens. Ports 1021 and 1022 were also assigned for SCTP and DCCP experimentation.
sections.eli5: Having an official number does not make a program safe. A guard should look at what is really coming through the door, not just at the number on it.
